outline.description: This chapter establishes the factual context of the dispute and outlines the relevant statutory provisions governing the Office of Special Counsel (OSC) and the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA). It details the specific conflict between America First Legal Foundation (AFL) and the Department of Justice (DOJ) regarding record production.
subtopics: Parties involved: America First Legal Foundation, Office of Special Counsel, and Department of Justice
The Civil Service Reform Act and OSC's investigative powers under 5 U.S.C. § 1216
FOIA enforcement provisions and OSC's role under 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(F)(i)
The underlying FOIA request: DOJ's policy on searching employee emails
OSC's refusal to investigate based on unmet statutory predicates

outline.description: This chapter traces the litigation path from the district court to the Court of Appeals. It highlights the district court's mixed ruling on OSC's authority and discretion, and explains why the appellate court prioritized the Article III standing question sua sponte.
subtopics: District court's ruling: Authority under § 1216 vs. Discretion under § 1216(c)
Remand to OSC and subsequent dismissal by the district court
AFL's appeal and the D.C. Circuit's de novo review
The court's sua sponte inquiry into Article III standing
Standing as a prerequisite for subject-matter jurisdiction

outline.chapter_title: Article III Standing Doctrine and Procedural Injuries
outline.description: This chapter outlines the constitutional and doctrinal requirements for Article III standing. It specifically focuses on the heightened scrutiny applied to claims based on procedural injuries, distinguishing between a right in vacuo and a right protecting a concrete interest.
subtopics: The three elements of standing: Injury in fact, causation, and redressability
The requirement for concrete and particularized injuries (Lujan standard)
Standing for procedural right violations (Summers v. Earth Island Inst.)
The relaxed standard for imminence and redressability in procedural injury cases
The necessity of a threatened concrete interest affected by the procedural deprivation

outline.chapter_title: Application of Standing Principles to AFL's Claims
outline.description: This chapter analyzes the court's application of standing doctrine to AFL's two specific theories. It examines why the causal chain regarding DOJ records was deemed too speculative and why the informational interest in OSC investigations lacked statutory entitlement.
subtopics: Theory One: Injury from DOJ's failure to produce FOIA records
Causation analysis: The speculative chain involving OSC, MSPB, and DOJ
Redressability analysis: Limitations of binding non-parties (DOJ) via OSC
Theory Two: Injury from lack of OSC investigation notices
Absence of statutory entitlement to information under § 1216
Discretionary nature of § 1214 notice requirements in § 1216 investigations

outline.description: This chapter summarizes the final holding and the disposition of the case. It discusses the broader implications for litigants seeking to compel OSC investigations and the limits of judicial power over agency enforcement discretion.
subtopics: Vacatur of the district court's judgment
Remand with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction
Implications for standing in FOIA-related OSC enforcement actions
The role of agency discretion in investigative proceedings (Heckler v. Chaney)
The boundary between judicial oversight and agency enforcement choices
